text: A psalm. A song for the dedication of the house. Of David.
I will exalt you, LORD, for you lifted me out of the depths and did not let my enemies gloat over me.
LORD my God, I cried to you for help, and you healed me.
LORD, you brought me up from the realm of the dead; you kept me alive so I would not go down to the pit.

versions.text: LORD, you brought me up from the grave; you spared me from going down to the pit.
versions.explanation: חִיִּיתַנִי means "you kept me alive / restored me to life," which is stronger and more concrete than "spared me." Also, שְׁאוֹל is better distinguished from בּוֹר ("pit") so the two lines are not both reduced to burial-place terms.

text: Sing to the LORD, you his faithful ones; give thanks to his holy name.
For his anger lasts only a moment, but his favor a lifetime. Weeping may spend the night, but joy comes in the morning.
When I felt secure, I said, "I will never be shaken."
LORD, in your favor you made my mountain stand firm; but when you hid your face, I was terrified.
To you, LORD, I called; to the Lord I pleaded for mercy:
"What is gained by my blood, if I go down to the pit? Can dust praise you? Can it proclaim your faithfulness?

versions.text: "What is gained if I am silenced, if I go down to the pit? Can dust praise you? Can it proclaim your faithfulness?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads "what profit is there in my blood" (בְּדָמִי), a reference to the psalmist's death, not to being silenced. Rendering it "if I am silenced" also anticipates and duplicates the verb יִדֹּם ("be silent") in verse 13, blurring the distinct imagery.

text: Hear me, LORD, and have mercy on me; LORD, be my helper."
You turned my mourning into dancing; you stripped off my sackcloth and clothed me with joy,
so that my glory may sing your praise and not be silent. LORD my God, I will thank you forever.

versions.text: so that my heart may sing your praise and not be silent. LORD my God, I will thank you forever.
versions.explanation: כָבוֹד here is "glory," a poetic term for the innermost self (compare Psalm 16:9). "Heart" is a reasonable paraphrase, but "glory" preserves the Hebrew image and can be clarified in a footnote if needed.
